entries.answer: In Nazareth, in Galilee. Jesus was born in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:1) and taken as a child to Egypt, then returned to “their own town of Nazareth” (Luke 2:39; Matthew 2:19-23). He lived there under Mary and Joseph and “grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man” (Luke 2:51-52). Luke 4:16 calls Nazareth the place “where He had been brought up”. People called Him “the carpenter” (Mark 6:3), and Matthew says that settling in Nazareth fulfilled what the prophets said, that He would be called a Nazarene (Matthew 2:23).

entries.question: Who were the twelve tribes of Israel?
alt_phrasings: what are the twelve tribes of israel

entries.answer: The twelve tribes descend from the sons of Jacob (Israel). Leah bore Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun; Bilhah bore Dan and Naphtali; Zilpah bore Gad and Asher; Rachel bore Joseph and Benjamin (Genesis 29:31-30:24; 35:16-26). In the land Joseph's tribe became two, Ephraim and Manasseh, whom Jacob adopted as his own sons (Genesis 48:5). Levi, the priestly tribe, received no territory but towns among the others (Joshua 13:14; 21:1-42). Jacob blessed each son in Genesis 49. Judah's tribe brought the kings and the Messiah (Genesis 49:10; Revelation 5:5). Revelation 7:4-8 lists the tribes again, with Manasseh in place of Dan.

entries.question: What happened to Lot's wife?

entries.answer: When God destroyed Sodom, angels led Lot, his wife and his two daughters out of the city and told them not to look back (Genesis 19:15-22). Lot's wife “looked back, and she became a pillar of salt” (Genesis 19:26). The Bible does not name her. Jesus uses her as a warning: “Remember Lot's wife!” (Luke 17:32), in a passage about not clinging to our possessions and our old life when He comes (Luke 17:28-33).

entries.question: What does amen mean?

meaning of amen
entries.answer: “Amen” is a Hebrew word from a root meaning firm and faithful; it means “truly” or “so be it”. The people of Israel answered “Amen” to the blessings and curses of the law (Deuteronomy 27:15-26), to praise (1 Chronicles 16:36; Psalm 106:48) and to the reading of the law (Nehemiah 8:6). Jesus began many sayings with “Amen” (“Truly I tell you”, Matthew 5:18), which marked what He said as certain. Christ is Himself “the Amen, the faithful and true Witness” (Revelation 3:14), and all God's promises are “Yes” in Him, so that through Him our “Amen” is spoken to the glory of God (2 Corinthians 1:20). The early church answered a prayer of thanks with “Amen” (1 Corinthians 14:16).

entries.question: Do angels have wings?
alt_phrasings: do angels have wings in the bible

entries.answer: Some do. The seraphim in Isaiah's vision have six wings (Isaiah 6:2), and the cherubim have wings, as on the cover of the ark (Ezekiel 1:5-11; Exodus 25:20). Gabriel is said to fly swiftly to Daniel (Daniel 9:21), and John sees an angel flying in midair (Revelation 14:6). But the Bible does not say that every angel has wings, and many angels simply appeared as men: the three visitors to Abraham (Genesis 18:2), the “young man dressed in a white robe” at the empty tomb (Mark 16:5), the “two men in radiant apparel” (Luke 24:4); we are told that some have entertained angels without knowing it (Hebrews 13:2). Angels are never described as babies.

entries.question: Who is Michael the archangel?
alt_phrasings: who is michael in the bible

entries.answer:
Scripture: Michael is called “one of the chief princes” (Daniel 10:13) and “your prince”, the great prince who stands guard over Daniel's people (Daniel 10:21; 12:1). Jude 9 calls him “the archangel Michael” who would not bring a slanderous accusation against the devil when they disputed over the body of Moses. In Revelation 12:7-9 Michael and his angels fight the dragon, and Paul says the Lord will come with “the voice of an archangel” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Gabriel, who stands in God's presence, brings messages to Daniel, Zechariah and Mary (Daniel 8:16; 9:21; Luke 1:19, 26).

Pentecostal understanding: Michael is a created angel, the chief angelic prince and warrior, and not Christ, who is far above the angels (Hebrews 1:4-14).

Other views: the Jehovah's Witnesses and some others identify Michael with the pre-human Christ; the mainstream church rejects that because Hebrews 1 shows the Son as greater than all the angels.

entries.question: How often should we fast?

entries.answer:
Scripture: the Bible gives no fixed number of fasts for Christians. Jesus speaks of fasting as expected: “When you fast” (not “if”), do it without show and the Father who sees in secret will reward you (Matthew 6:16-18), and He said that when the Bridegroom is taken away His disciples will fast (Matthew 9:14-15). The only fast required by the Law was on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29-31). The church fasted when seeking God's direction (Acts 13:2-3; 14:23). Isaiah describes the fast God chooses: to loose the chains of injustice and share bread with the hungry (Isaiah 58:6-9). Examples include Esther's three days (Esther 4:16) and Jesus' forty days (Matthew 4:2).

Pentecostal understanding: fasting with prayer is a regular practice of the Spirit-filled life, often one day a week or for set seasons and special needs, with water or a partial fast for those who cannot go without food.

Other views: many traditions fast at set seasons such as Lent, and others leave the frequency and form to each believer's conscience.

entries.answer: “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). The LORD hates pride and arrogance (Proverbs 8:13), and “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). Scripture shows the downfall of pride in the king of Tyre (Ezekiel 28:17), the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:12-15) and Nebuchadnezzar, who was humbled until he praised God (Daniel 4:30-37). Jesus told of the Pharisee who prayed about himself while the tax collector begged for mercy, and said that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled (Luke 18:9-14). John calls “the pride of life” something that is not from the Father (1 John 2:16). Paul says to do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, but in humility to value others above ourselves, as Christ did (Philippians 2:3-8).

entries.answer: Genesis says that the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and a river flowed out of it and divided into four: the Pishon, which winds through the land of Havilah; the Gihon, which winds through Cush; the Tigris (Hiddekel), east of Assyria; and the Euphrates (Genesis 2:8-14). The Bible does not give a map location that we can find today, and the flood and the curse changed the earth. The Tigris and Euphrates point to Mesopotamia, where many place it, but two of the four rivers cannot be identified with certainty. The tree of life, shut out after the fall (Genesis 3:22-24), returns in the new creation (Revelation 22:1-2).

entries.answer: Genesis says that in the seventh month the ark came to rest “on the mountains of Ararat” (Genesis 8:4). Ararat is a region, not one named peak: the Bible later speaks of the “land of Ararat” (2 Kings 19:37; Isaiah 37:38), which was the kingdom of Urartu in the highlands of what is now eastern Turkey and Armenia. Tradition identifies the peak now called Mount Ararat (Agri Dagi) in eastern Turkey, but the Bible does not name the exact mountain, and no one has proved a find of the ark.

entries.question: Who was John the Baptist?

entries.answer: John the Baptist was the son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth, born after the angel Gabriel promised his parents a son who would be filled with the Holy Spirit from the womb (Luke 1:5-25, 57-63). He lived in the wilderness, wore a garment of camel's hair and ate locusts and wild honey (Matthew 3:4). He preached repentance and baptized in the Jordan, preparing the way for the Lord as Isaiah had foretold (Matthew 3:1-6; Isaiah 40:3). He baptized Jesus (Matthew 3:13-17) and pointed to Him as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). He rebuked Herod Antipas for taking his brother's wife and was beheaded (Mark 6:17-29). Jesus said that no one born of women was greater than John (Matthew 11:11) and that he was the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14).

entries.answer: Deborah was a prophetess and a judge of Israel, the wife of Lappidoth. She sat under the palm of Deborah in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites came to her for judgment (Judges 4:4-5). At God's word she called Barak to gather ten thousand men against Sisera, the commander of the Canaanite king Jabin, who had oppressed Israel for twenty years (Judges 4:3, 6-7). Barak would go only if she went with him, and she told him that the honour of the victory would go to a woman (Judges 4:8-10). The LORD routed Sisera's army, and Jael killed Sisera in her tent (Judges 4:14-22). Deborah and Barak sang a song of victory (Judges 5), and the land had peace for forty years (Judges 5:31). A different Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, is mentioned in Genesis 35:8.

entries.question: Who was Elijah?

entries.answer: Elijah the Tishbite was a prophet of Israel in the days of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel (1 Kings 17:1). He declared a drought, was fed by ravens at the brook Cherith, and for a widow in Zarephath the jar of flour and the jug of oil did not run out; he raised her son (1 Kings 17:2-24). On Mount Carmel he challenged the prophets of Baal, and fire fell from heaven on his sacrifice (1 Kings 18:20-39). Fleeing Jezebel, he met God not in the wind, earthquake or fire but in a gentle whisper at Horeb (1 Kings 19:11-13). He called Elisha to follow him (1 Kings 19:19-21) and was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind with chariots and horses of fire (2 Kings 2:11). Malachi promised that Elijah would come before the great day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5-6), and Jesus said that John the Baptist was that Elijah (Matthew 11:14). Elijah appeared with Moses at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1-3), and James holds him up as a man of powerful prayer (James 5:16-18).

entries.question: What was the tabernacle?

entries.answer: The tabernacle was the portable tent sanctuary that God commanded Moses to build in the wilderness, so that He could live among His people (Exodus 25:8-9). It was made to the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain (Exodus 25:9, 40). It had an outer court with the bronze altar and basin, a Holy Place with the lampstand, the table of the bread of the Presence and the altar of incense, and behind a veil the Most Holy Place with the ark of the covenant (Exodus 25-27; 30). When it was finished the cloud covered it and the glory of the LORD filled it (Exodus 40:34-35). It was later replaced by Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8). The New Testament sees it as a copy and shadow of heavenly things (Hebrews 8:5; 9:23-24); Christ entered the greater and more perfect tabernacle by His own blood (Hebrews 9:11-12), and John says that the Word became flesh and “made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14), a word that echoes the tabernacle (the Greek verb means to pitch a tent).

entries.question: Who wrote the Bible?

entries.answer: The Bible is a library of 66 books written by about forty human authors over some 1,500 years: Moses wrote the first five books (Exodus 24:4; Deuteronomy 31:9), David and others the psalms, Solomon much of the wisdom writings, the prophets their own books, and Matthew, Mark, Luke and John the four Gospels (Luke 1:1-4; John 21:24). Paul wrote many of the letters, with letters also by Peter, James, John and Jude; Hebrews is anonymous. Yet Scripture says that God is the source: “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16), and “men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21).

entries.question: What does the Bible say about forgiveness?

entries.answer: God forgives those who come to Him: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). In Christ we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of sins (Ephesians 1:7), and God removes our sins from us as far as the east is from the west (Psalm 103:12). We are told to forgive in the same way: “forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32; Colossians 3:13). Jesus said that if we forgive others our Father will forgive us, but if we do not forgive, neither will He forgive our sins (Matthew 6:14-15); when we stand praying we are to forgive anyone we hold something against (Mark 11:25). We are to forgive again and again (Matthew 18:21-22; Luke 17:3-4). Jesus forgave His killers from the cross (Luke 23:34), and Stephen did the same (Acts 7:60).

entries.question: Who was Pontius Pilate?
alt_phrasings: who was pilate

entries.answer: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea in the days of Tiberius Caesar (Luke 3:1), the official before whom the Jewish leaders brought Jesus (Matthew 27:11-26; John 18:28-19:16). Pilate asked Him whether He was the King of the Jews and said three times that he found no guilt in Him (John 18:38; Luke 23:4, 14-22); his wife warned him about Jesus after a dream (Matthew 27:19). Fearing the crowd, he washed his hands before them and handed Jesus over to be crucified (Matthew 27:24-26), and he had the notice “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews” fixed to the cross (John 19:19). He later allowed Joseph of Arimathea to bury the body and set a guard at the tomb (Mark 15:43-45; Matthew 27:62-66). The rest of Pilate's life is told outside the Bible.

entries.question: What does shalom mean?

entries.answer: Shalom is the Hebrew word for peace, but it means much more than the absence of war: wholeness, health, safety and well-being in every part of life. It is used as a greeting and a farewell, “Peace be with you” (Judges 6:23), and in asking after someone's welfare (Genesis 43:27). Gideon named his altar “The LORD Is Peace” (Judges 6:24). The priestly blessing asks the LORD to look on His people with favour and give them peace (Numbers 6:24-26). The Messiah is the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6); God keeps in perfect peace the one whose mind is stayed on Him (Isaiah 26:3). Jesus said, “Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you” (John 14:27), and the peace of God guards the hearts and minds of those who pray (Philippians 4:6-7).

entries.question: What does the name Jesus mean?
alt_phrasings: what is the meaning of the name jesus

entries.answer: “Jesus” is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Yeshua (Joshua), which means “the LORD saves”. The angel told Joseph, “you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21; Luke 1:31). “Christ” is not a surname but a title: the Greek for the Hebrew Messiah, the Anointed One (John 1:41). Matthew also records the name Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23; Isaiah 7:14). God has given Him the name above every name, at which every knee will bow (Philippians 2:9-11), and there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12).

entries.question: What is the body of Christ?

entries.answer: The body of Christ is the church, all believers joined to Him and to one another. Christ is its head (Colossians 1:18; Ephesians 1:22-23). “The body is a unit, though it is composed of many parts. And although its parts are many, they all form one body. So it is with Christ” (1 Corinthians 12:12): by one Spirit we were all baptized into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). Each member has a different gift and is needed; no part can say to another, “I do not need you” (1 Corinthians 12:14-27; Romans 12:4-8). Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers to equip the saints until the body grows up in love (Ephesians 4:11-16). In Communion the bread is also called a sharing in the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16-17).

entries.question: What was the Holy of Holies?

entries.answer: The Holy of Holies, or Most Holy Place, was the inner room of the tabernacle and later of the temple, separated from the Holy Place by a veil (Exodus 26:33-34; 1 Kings 6:16, 19). It held the ark of the covenant with the mercy seat between the cherubim, where God said He would meet with Moses and speak (Exodus 25:22). Only the high priest could enter, once a year on the Day of Atonement, and not without blood (Leviticus 16:2, 12-15; Hebrews 9:7). When Jesus died the temple veil was torn in two from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51), and Hebrews says that “we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19-22; 9:11-12).

entries.question: What are the seven churches in Revelation?
alt_phrasings: who are the seven churches of revelation
what were the seven churches of asia
list the seven churches in revelation
what are the letters to the seven churches
what did jesus say to the seven churches
entries.answer:
Scripture: Jesus told John to write to seven churches in Asia (what is now western Turkey): Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea (Revelation 1:11; chapters 2-3). Ephesus had left its first love (2:4). Smyrna was faithful in suffering and was promised the crown of life (2:10). Pergamum stayed faithful but tolerated false teaching (2:14-15). Thyatira grew in love and service but tolerated the false prophetess Jezebel (2:19-20). Sardis had a reputation of being alive but was dead (3:1). Philadelphia had little strength but had kept His word and was given an open door (3:8). Laodicea was lukewarm and was told to buy gold refined by fire and to open the door to Christ (3:15-20). Each letter ends with a promise to the one who overcomes.

Pentecostal understanding: they were real churches that received a real letter, and each also warns the church of every age, so that a church or a believer who goes cold, compromises or grows lukewarm must repent; many Pentecostal and dispensational teachers also see in the seven a picture of the stages of church history.

Other views: many read the seven only as the churches of John's day, with lessons for all churches; others take the seven as a symbol of the whole church (seven being the number of completeness).

entries.question: What is the Book of Life?
alt_phrasings: what is the book of life in revelation

entries.answer:
Scripture: the Book of Life is the record of those who belong to God. Jesus told His disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20), and Paul speaks of fellow workers whose names are in the book of life (Philippians 4:3). Revelation says that whoever's name is not found written in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:12, 15), and that nothing unclean will enter the New Jerusalem, only those written in the Lamb's book of life (Revelation 21:27). Jesus promises the one who overcomes that He will never blot out his name from the book of life, but will acknowledge it before the Father (Revelation 3:5); Moses and the psalmist also speak of names blotted out (Exodus 32:32-33; Psalm 69:28).

Pentecostal understanding: the names of the born-again are written there through the blood of the Lamb, and the warnings of Scripture show that a believer who willfully turns away from Christ and does not overcome is at risk (Exodus 32:33; Revelation 3:5).

Other views: Reformed and others hold that the names were written before the foundation of the world and can never be removed (Revelation 13:8; 17:8), so that those who seem to fall away were never truly written there.

entries.question: What is the lake of fire?
alt_phrasings: what is the second death
what is the lake of fire in revelation

what is the second death in revelation
entries.answer:
Scripture: the lake of fire is the final place of judgment. The beast and the false prophet are thrown into it alive (Revelation 19:20), the devil is thrown in and tormented day and night forever (Revelation 20:10), and then Death and Hades, and anyone whose name was not found in the book of life (Revelation 20:14-15). Revelation calls it the second death and names the cowardly, unbelieving, murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters and all liars among those who face it (Revelation 21:8). Jesus said that it was prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41), and that the wicked go away to eternal punishment and the righteous to eternal life (Matthew 25:46). The second death has no power over those who share in the first resurrection (Revelation 20:6) or the one who overcomes (Revelation 2:11).

Pentecostal understanding: it is a real place of everlasting separation from God for the devil and for all who finally reject Christ, which is why the gospel must be preached.

Other views: some Christians (annihilationists) hold that the lost are destroyed rather than tormented without end; a few hold that all will finally be saved; some read the fire as a picture of God's judgment rather than a literal flame.

entries.question: How can I hear God's voice?
alt_phrasings: how do i hear god's voice

entries.answer:
Scripture: God has spoken most fully through His Son (Hebrews 1:1-2) and through His written Word, which is a lamp to our feet (Psalm 119:105; 2 Timothy 3:16-17). Jesus said that His sheep listen to His voice (John 10:27) and promised that the Holy Spirit would guide us into all the truth and tell us what is to come (John 16:13). The Spirit testifies with our spirit that we are God's children (Romans 8:14-16), God spoke to Elijah in a gentle whisper (1 Kings 19:12), and God gives gifts of the Spirit, including prophecy, for the building up of the church (1 Corinthians 12:7-11; 14:1-3). We are to be still before Him (Psalm 46:10), to pray, and to test every spirit and every word (1 John 4:1; 1 Thessalonians 5:19-21).

Pentecostal understanding: the Spirit still speaks, first through the Bible, then by an inward witness, prophecy, a word of knowledge and sometimes dreams or visions (Acts 2:17), and all of it must agree with Scripture and be tested by mature believers.

entries.question: How did the apostle Paul die?
alt_phrasings: where did paul die

entries.answer: The Bible does not record Paul's death. Acts ends with Paul in Rome under house arrest, welcoming all who came to him and proclaiming the kingdom of God for two years (Acts 28:30-31). In his last letter he writes, “For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is near,” and he looks ahead to the crown of righteousness that the Lord will give to all who love His appearing (2 Timothy 4:6-8). Early Christian tradition outside the Bible says that he was beheaded in Rome under the emperor Nero, about AD 64 to 67.

entries.answer: The Bible gives Jesus no middle name, and middle names were not the custom in His day. He was named Jesus at the angel's word (Matthew 1:21; Luke 1:31), and people identified Him by His town or His family: “Jesus of Nazareth” (John 1:45; Acts 2:22) and “the son of Joseph” (Luke 3:23; John 6:42). “Christ” is not a middle name or a surname but the title Messiah, the Anointed One (John 1:41).

entries.answer: Isaac was the son of Abraham and Sarah, born when Abraham was a hundred years old and Sarah far past the age of bearing, as God had promised (Genesis 17:15-19; 21:1-5). His name means “he laughs”, and Sarah said that God had made her laugh (Genesis 21:6). God tested Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac on Mount Moriah, then stopped his hand and provided a ram instead (Genesis 22:1-14). Isaac married Rebekah (Genesis 24:62-67) and was the father of the twins Esau and Jacob (Genesis 25:19-26). God renewed to him the covenant made with Abraham (Genesis 26:2-5), and he died at the age of 180 (Genesis 35:28-29). The New Testament calls him the child of promise (Galatians 4:28) and sees in his offering a picture of faith in the God who raises the dead (Hebrews 11:17-19).

entries.answer: David was the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, a shepherd whom the prophet Samuel anointed as king (1 Samuel 16:1-13). He killed the giant Goliath (1 Samuel 17), served King Saul and fled from his jealousy (1 Samuel 18-27), then became king of Judah at Hebron and of all Israel, and took Jerusalem (2 Samuel 2:4; 5:1-9). He brought the ark to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6), and God promised him a house and a throne that would last forever (2 Samuel 7:12-16). He sinned with Bathsheba and against her husband Uriah, and repented (2 Samuel 11-12; Psalm 51). God called him “a man after My own heart” (Acts 13:22), and he wrote many of the psalms. He reigned forty years (2 Samuel 5:4). Jesus is the promised Son of David (Matthew 1:1; Luke 1:32).

entries.question: Who was the prophet Daniel?

entries.answer: Daniel was a young Jewish nobleman taken to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, trained in the king's service, and kept faithful to God, refusing the king's food (Daniel 1:1-16). God gave him wisdom to interpret dreams, including Nebuchadnezzar's great statue (Daniel 2) and the tree that was cut down (Daniel 4), and he read the writing on the wall for Belshazzar (Daniel 5). He served under both Babylon and Persia (Daniel 6:1-3). Because he prayed three times a day to God, he was thrown into the lions' den and was delivered (Daniel 6). He received visions of the four beasts, the Son of Man and the seventy weeks (Daniel 7; 9:24-27). Ezekiel names him with Noah and Job as a righteous man (Ezekiel 14:14), and Jesus speaks of “the prophet Daniel” (Matthew 24:15).

entries.question: Who was the prophet Jeremiah?

entries.answer: Jeremiah was a prophet and priest from Anathoth, the son of Hilkiah, whom God called while he was still young (Jeremiah 1:1-10). For some forty years he warned Judah to turn back to God before Jerusalem fell to Babylon, and he was mocked, beaten, put in the stocks, imprisoned and thrown into a cistern (Jeremiah 20:1-2; 37-38). His grief for his people has earned him the name of the weeping prophet (Jeremiah 9:1). He foretold seventy years of exile (Jeremiah 25:11-12; 29:10) and wrote to the exiles that God had “plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope” (Jeremiah 29:11). He promised the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34), which Jesus established in His blood (Luke 22:20). Tradition says he also wrote Lamentations.

entries.question: Who was the prophet Ezekiel?

entries.answer: Ezekiel was a priest, the son of Buzi, who was taken to Babylon in the exile of 597 BC and called to be a prophet by the Chebar canal (Ezekiel 1:1-3; 2:1-3). He saw the glory of the LORD in a vision of living creatures, wheels and a throne (Ezekiel 1). God made him a watchman for Israel (Ezekiel 3:17; 33:7). He foretold the fall of Jerusalem, often through signs acted out before the people (Ezekiel 4-24), spoke against the nations (Ezekiel 25-32), and then promised restoration: a new heart and God's Spirit within His people (Ezekiel 36:26-27), the valley of dry bones brought to life (Ezekiel 37), the war of Gog and Magog (Ezekiel 38-39) and the vision of a new temple (Ezekiel 40-48).

entries.question: Who was Lydia in the Bible?

entries.answer: Lydia was a woman from the city of Thyatira who sold purple cloth and lived in Philippi. She worshipped God, and when Paul spoke to the women by the river outside the city on the Sabbath, the Lord opened her heart to respond to his message (Acts 16:13-14). She and her household were baptized, and she urged Paul and his companions to stay in her home (Acts 16:15). After Paul and Silas were released from prison, they met with the believers at her house (Acts 16:40). She is the first person in Europe whose conversion is recorded.

entries.answer: Rahab was a prostitute in Jericho who hid the two Israelite spies on her roof and sent the king's men in the wrong direction (Joshua 2:1-7). She told the spies that the LORD had given the land to Israel and that He is God in heaven above and on earth below, and she asked that her family be spared (Joshua 2:8-13). She tied a scarlet cord in her window (Joshua 2:18-21). When the walls fell she and all her family were saved (Joshua 6:17, 22-25). She went on to marry Salmon of the tribe of Judah and became the mother of Boaz, who married Ruth, and so an ancestor of King David and of Jesus: “Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab, Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, Obed the father of Jesse” (Matthew 1:5; Ruth 4:20-22; 1 Chronicles 2:11). Salmon was the son of Nahshon, the leader of Judah (Numbers 1:7). Matthew does not add “of Jericho”, and the Bible does not say how or when Rahab and Salmon married, but the church has always understood the Rahab of Matthew 1:5 to be the woman of Jericho, as the Bible dictionaries of Easton and Smith also say. Only four generations stand between Rahab and David, which is a short span for the time, but Bible genealogies often leave out names (compare Matthew 1:8 with 1 Chronicles 3:11-12). She is honoured for her faith (Hebrews 11:31) and for her works (James 2:25).

entries.answer: Joseph was the eleventh son of Jacob, the firstborn of Rachel, and his father's favourite. His brothers hated him for his dreams and his special coat, and sold him to traders who took him to Egypt (Genesis 37). In Potiphar's house he was falsely accused and imprisoned, but the LORD was with him (Genesis 39). He interpreted the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker and then Pharaoh's dream of seven good years and seven years of famine, and Pharaoh made him ruler over Egypt at the age of thirty (Genesis 40-41). When his brothers came to buy grain he tested them and then forgave them: “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (Genesis 50:20; chapters 42-45). Jacob's family settled in Egypt (Genesis 46-47), and Joseph died at 110, asking that his bones be taken to the promised land (Genesis 50:22-26; Exodus 13:19).

entries.question: Who was Mary, the mother of Jesus?
alt_phrasings: who was mary
tell me about mary the mother of jesus
who was the virgin mary
what does the bible say about mary
who was mary in the bible
was mary a virgin
entries.answer:
Scripture: Mary was a young virgin of Nazareth, engaged to Joseph, to whom the angel Gabriel said, “you who are highly favored”, and told her that she would conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear the Son of the Most High (Luke 1:26-38; Matthew 1:18-23). Elizabeth called her blessed because she believed (Luke 1:42-45), and she answered in her song of praise (Luke 1:46-55). She gave birth to Jesus in Bethlehem (Luke 2:1-7), heard Simeon's warning that a sword would pierce her soul (Luke 2:34-35), asked Jesus for help at the wedding in Cana (John 2:1-5), stood by the cross, where Jesus entrusted her to the care of John (John 19:25-27), and was among the believers praying in the upper room (Acts 1:14).

Pentecostal understanding: Mary is honoured as the blessed virgin chosen to bear the Savior and as an example of faith and obedience, but she is a believer saved by Christ like the rest of us, and is not to be worshipped or prayed to, because there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). She was a virgin when Jesus was conceived and born, but the Gospels' own words point to a normal married life afterward. Matthew 1:25 says that Joseph “had no union with her until she gave birth to a Son”, and the word “until” suggests that they came together afterward. Luke 2:7 calls Jesus her “firstborn, a Son”, which suggests that other children followed, and the people of Nazareth named Jesus' brothers and sisters (Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55-56).

Other views: Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches honour her as the Mother of God (Theotokos), and Catholics teach her immaculate conception, perpetual virginity and assumption into heaven, and ask for her prayers; most Protestants honour her but reject those teachings.

entries.question: Who was James, the brother of Jesus?

entries.answer:
Scripture: the people of Nazareth named Jesus' brothers: James, Joseph, Simon and Judas, and His sisters (Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55). During His ministry His brothers did not believe in Him (John 7:5), but Jesus appeared to James after the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:7), and His brothers were among the believers praying in the upper room (Acts 1:14). Paul met “James, the Lord's brother” in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19) and counted him one of the pillars of the church (Galatians 2:9). James spoke at the council of Jerusalem (Acts 15:13-21) and wrote the letter of James (James 1:1); his brother Jude wrote the letter of Jude (Jude 1). Tradition says he was martyred in Jerusalem about AD 62.

Pentecostal understanding: they were younger half-brothers of Jesus, sons of Joseph and Mary born after Jesus (Matthew 1:25; Luke 2:7).

Other views: the Orthodox churches hold that they were Joseph's children from an earlier marriage, and the Catholic Church that they were close relatives (cousins), since both teach that Mary remained a virgin all her life.

entries.answer: Joseph was a descendant of David from Nazareth, a carpenter (Matthew 1:20; 13:55), and a righteous man who did not want to expose Mary to public disgrace when he learned that she was expecting (Matthew 1:19). An angel told him in a dream to take Mary as his wife and to name the child Jesus, and he obeyed (Matthew 1:20-25). He took Mary to Bethlehem for the census (Luke 2:4-7), fled with the child to Egypt after a warning in a dream (Matthew 2:13-15), and brought the family back to Nazareth (Matthew 2:19-23). He took Jesus to Jerusalem at twelve (Luke 2:41-52). He is not mentioned after that, and the Bible does not say when he died. People spoke of Jesus as the son of Joseph (Luke 3:23; John 6:42).

entries.answer: The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) was the holiest day of Israel's year, on the tenth day of the seventh month. Israel was to deny themselves and do no work, because on that day atonement was made to cleanse them from all their sins before the LORD (Leviticus 16:29-31; 23:26-32). Once a year the high priest, after offering a sacrifice for himself, entered the Most Holy Place with the blood of a bull and of a goat and sprinkled it on the mercy seat (Leviticus 16:3-17). The second goat, the scapegoat, had the sins of the people confessed over it and was sent away into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:7-10, 20-22). Hebrews says that Christ has entered the heavenly Most Holy Place once for all, not with the blood of goats and calves but with His own blood, having obtained eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:7-14, 24-28).

entries.answer:
Scripture: the Feast of Tabernacles (Booths, Sukkot) began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and lasted seven days. Israel was to live in booths made of branches so that their descendants would know that God had made them live in booths when He brought them out of Egypt, and they were to rejoice before the LORD (Leviticus 23:33-43; Deuteronomy 16:13-15). At this feast Jesus stood and cried out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink” (John 7:2, 37-38). Zechariah foretells that the survivors of the nations will go up each year to Jerusalem to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts, and to keep this feast (Zechariah 14:16-19).

Pentecostal understanding: many see in the feast a picture of the coming kingdom, when Christ reigns on earth and God dwells among His people (Zechariah 14:9, 16; Revelation 21:3).

Other views: others see it fulfilled in Christ, who “made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14), and in the church as God's dwelling by the Spirit.

entries.question: What does it mean that we are made in the image of God?
alt_phrasings: what is the image of god

entries.answer: Scripture: God said, “Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness,” and made them male and female (Genesis 1:26-27). Even after the fall that image is not lost: taking human life is forbidden because man was made in God's image (Genesis 9:6), and James says people are made in God's likeness (James 3:9). Christ is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15; 2 Corinthians 4:4). Believers are being renewed in knowledge after the image of their Creator (Colossians 3:10; Ephesians 4:24), are being transformed into the Lord's image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18), and will be conformed to the image of His Son (Romans 8:29; 1 Corinthians 15:49). The Bible does not define the image in a single sentence. The church has understood it as our ability to know and love God, our moral sense, our rule over creation and our relationships, so that the whole person, not any one part, bears God's image.

entries.answer:
Scripture: righteousness is being right with God and living right before Him. God Himself is righteous (Psalm 119:137; 145:17). No one is righteous in himself, for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:10, 23). But God's righteousness is given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe (Romans 3:21-26; Philippians 3:9): “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Believers are called to live it: to offer ourselves to God as instruments of righteousness (Romans 6:13, 18), to practice it (1 John 3:7), and to hunger and thirst for it (Matthew 5:6) and seek it first with God's kingdom (Matthew 6:33).

Pentecostal understanding: righteousness is God's gift through faith in the blood of Jesus, and the born-again are called to live it out in the power of the Spirit (Romans 8:4; 1 John 3:7).

Other views: Reformed and Lutheran teaching holds that Christ's righteousness is counted as ours once and for all (imputed); Roman Catholic teaching holds that righteousness is also poured into the believer and grows through the sacraments.

entries.question: What is the soul?
alt_phrasings: what is the human soul

entries.answer:
Scripture: God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being (Genesis 2:7). The word the Old Testament uses for soul (nephesh) often means the life or the whole person. Jesus said, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul,” but fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell (Matthew 10:28), and asked what it profits a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul (Matthew 16:26). We are to love God with all our heart, soul, mind and strength (Mark 12:30), and the psalmist speaks to his own soul: “Bless the LORD, O my soul” (Psalm 103:1). Paul prays, “Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely, and may your entire spirit, soul, and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:23), and the word of God divides soul and spirit (Hebrews 4:12).

Pentecostal understanding: a person is spirit, soul and body: the spirit is where we meet God and are born again, the soul is the mind, will and emotions, and the soul is eternal and must be saved (James 1:21; 1 Peter 1:9).

Other views: many teachers hold that soul and spirit are two names for the one inner life (dichotomy); others hold that the Bible speaks of the whole person and that “soul” means the life of the person (monism); Roman Catholic teaching holds that each soul is created by God and immortal.

entries.answer: Genesis, the first book of the Bible, is traditionally ascribed to Moses. It tells of the beginning: the creation of the world, the fall of man, the flood, the call of Abraham, and the stories of Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, ending with Israel's family in Egypt. It shows God as the Creator who makes a people for Himself by promise. Key verse: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” (Genesis 1:1).

It tells how God freed Israel from slavery in Egypt through the ten plagues and the Passover, brought them through the Red Sea, gave the law at Mount Sinai and had the tabernacle built so that He could live among them. Key verse: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” (Exodus 20:2).

entries.answer: Leviticus is traditionally ascribed to Moses. It sets out the laws of sacrifice and priesthood, the Day of Atonement, clean and unclean, and the feasts. Key verse: “Speak to the whole congregation of Israel and tell them: Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy.” (Leviticus 19:2).

entries.answer: Numbers is traditionally ascribed to Moses. It records Israel's counting and their forty years in the wilderness: the unbelief at Kadesh, the death of that generation, and a new generation brought to the edge of the promised land. It shows God's faithfulness in spite of Israel's complaining. Key verse: “May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace.'” (Numbers 6:24-26).

entries.answer: Deuteronomy is traditionally ascribed to Moses. It is Moses' farewell speech on the plains of Moab: a review of the journey, the law repeated, and the covenant renewed with its blessings and curses, with the call to love the LORD and choose life. It ends with Moses' death. Key verse: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One. And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength.” (Deuteronomy 6:4-5).

entries.answer: Judges is traditionally ascribed to Samuel. It records his vision of God's glory, his warnings of Jerusalem's fall, judgments on the nations, and then the promise of restoration: a new heart and Spirit, the valley of dry bones, and a new temple. entries.answer:
Scripture: Daniel is the work of the prophet Daniel, who served in Babylon and Persia. Its first half tells of Daniel and his friends: the fiery furnace, the writing on the wall and the lions' den. Its second half records visions of four world kingdoms, the Son of Man receiving an everlasting kingdom, and the seventy weeks. Key verse: “If the God whom we serve exists, then He is able to deliver us from the blazing fiery furnace and from your hand, O king. But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up.” (Daniel 3:17-18).

Pentecostal understanding: the visions of Daniel look ahead to the last days, including the coming of the Antichrist (Daniel 9:27; 11:36-45) and Christ's everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13-14), and Daniel 12:1-3 points to the great tribulation and the resurrection.

Other views: many scholars date the visions to the second century BC and read them as pointing to Antiochus Epiphanes; preterist teachers see the fulfilment in the first century, and historicists in the whole sweep of church history.

entries.answer:
Scripture: Joel is the work of the prophet Joel. After a plague of locusts, Joel calls the people to repent and warns of the day of the LORD. He promises that God will pour out His Spirit on all people. Key verse: “And afterward, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions.” (Joel 2:28).

Pentecostal understanding: Peter quoted this promise on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:16-21) as the outpouring of the Spirit that began then and goes on for all who call on the Lord, and which points ahead to the signs before the day of the LORD.

Other views: some hold that Joel's promise was fully fulfilled at Pentecost; others that its final fulfilment is still future for Israel.

entries.answer:
Scripture: Acts (the Acts of the Apostles) was written by Luke as the second part of his Gospel. It tells of the ascension, the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, and the spread of the gospel from Jerusalem through Judea and Samaria to Rome, through Peter, Stephen, Philip and above all Paul. Key verse: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.” (Acts 1:8).

Pentecostal understanding: Acts is the pattern for the church in every age, with the baptism in the Holy Spirit and speaking in tongues (Acts 2:4; 10:44-46; 19:6), healings, signs and wonders, which are for us today (Acts 2:38-39).

Other views: cessationist teachers hold that Acts records the unique days of the apostles and is not a pattern for today; others take Acts as a record of what happened and a guide to the church's mission, but not a rule for each believer's experience.

entries.answer:
Scripture: 1 Corinthians is a letter from the apostle Paul to the church in Corinth. He answers reports of divisions, immorality, lawsuits and abuses at the Lord's Supper, teaches about marriage, idols and spiritual gifts (chapters 12-14), gives the chapter on love (chapter 13), and defends the resurrection (chapter 15). Key verse: “And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love.” (1 Corinthians 13:13).

Pentecostal understanding: chapters 12 and 14 teach that the gifts of the Spirit, including tongues, interpretation and prophecy, are given to the church and are for today (1 Corinthians 12:7-11; 14:1-5, 39), and that love must rule their use (1 Corinthians 13).

Other views: cessationist teachers read 1 Corinthians 13:8-10 as saying that some gifts ended with the apostles and the completed Scriptures; others hold that all the gifts continue until Christ returns.

entries.answer: 1 John is a letter traditionally ascribed to the apostle John. entries.answer:
Scripture: Revelation was written by John while he was exiled on the island of Patmos. It opens with letters to seven churches, then shows the throne of God, the seals, trumpets and bowls of judgment, the Antichrist, the return of Christ, the thousand years, the final judgment, and the new heaven and new earth. Key verse: “He who testifies to these things says, Yes, I am coming soon. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

Pentecostal understanding: most of the book looks ahead to the Rapture, the Tribulation, the return of Christ in glory, the thousand-year reign and the final judgment, in the order held by pre-tribulation, premillennial believers.

Other views: amillennial and postmillennial teachers read the thousand years as the present age or a golden age before Christ returns; preterists see most of it fulfilled in the first century, and historicists in the history of the church.

entries.answer: Jesus of Nazareth is the Son of God, who became a man, died for our sins, rose again on the third day, and will come again. John writes that in the beginning was the Word, “and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and that “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:1, 14). He is “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation” (Colossians 1:15), and “the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature” (Hebrews 1:3). Though He existed in the form of God, He “emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,” and was obedient even to death on a cross (Philippians 2:6-8). He was born of the virgin Mary in Bethlehem (Matthew 1:18-25; Luke 2:1-7), taught and healed, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, was buried and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). “Christ” means the Anointed One, the promised Messiah (Matthew 16:16), and the name Jesus tells us that He will save His people from their sins (Matthew 1:21). John wrote his Gospel “so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name” (John 20:31). Jesus said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6).

entries.answer:
Scripture: “But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). “He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness” (1 Peter 2:24). “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Jesus said that the Son of Man came “to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). “Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” (Hebrews 9:22), and God “sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 4:10). On the cross He also disarmed the powers and authorities, “triumphing over them by the cross” (Colossians 2:15). Isaiah foretold that He was “pierced for our transgressions” and that “by His stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).

Pentecostal understanding: Jesus died in our place, bearing the punishment our sins deserved, so that we could be forgiven, made righteous and reconciled to God (Romans 3:23-26); He also defeated Satan, sin and death, and, as Isaiah 53:5 and 1 Peter 2:24 say, His stripes have provided for our healing (Matthew 8:16-17).

Other views: the Church has always used several pictures of the cross, a ransom, a sacrifice, a victory over evil (Hebrews 2:14-15), and a demonstration of love that draws us to God (Romans 5:8; John 12:32); different traditions stress different ones. Roman Catholic teaching speaks of Christ making satisfaction for sin, the Eastern Orthodox emphasise His victory over death and the healing of human nature, and many Reformed teachers stress that He bore the penalty in our place. Many Christians do not hold that healing is guaranteed in the atonement in the same way.

entries.answer: The word gospel means good news. Paul sums it up: “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Jesus began His ministry by saying, “The time is fulfilled,” and, “the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!” (Mark 1:15). Paul wrote, “I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (Romans 1:16), and “if you confess with your mouth, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9). We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works (Ephesians 2:8-9). The good news is that God has forgiven sinners and offers eternal life through Jesus Christ, who died in our place and rose again, and that the kingdom of God is open to all who repent and believe (John 3:16; Acts 2:38).

entries.answer:
Scripture: Jesus told Nicodemus, “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again” (John 3:3), and “no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and the Spirit. Flesh is born of flesh, but spirit is born of the Spirit” (John 3:5-6). Peter writes, “you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God” (1 Peter 1:23). Paul says that God “saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5), and that “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!” (2 Corinthians 5:17). God had promised through Ezekiel, “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26-27).

Pentecostal understanding: being born again is the work of the Holy Spirit, who makes a person alive to God when he repents of his sins and puts his faith in Christ; he receives a new heart, becomes a child of God (John 1:12-13; 1 John 5:1), and is a new creation. This is a different experience from the baptism in the Holy Spirit, which Pentecostals teach is given for power to witness.

Other views: the Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican churches generally understand the “water” of John 3:5 as baptism and teach that new birth is given in baptism, including to infants. Many Reformed and evangelical teachers read “water and the Spirit” in the light of Ezekiel 36:25-27 as the cleansing and renewing work of the Spirit, and say that God gives new life before a person can believe.

entries.answer: To repent is to change one's mind about sin and turn back to God. The Greek word (metanoia) means a change of mind that leads to a change of direction. Jesus began His ministry by saying, “Repent and believe in the gospel!” (Mark 1:15), and warned, “unless you repent, you too will all perish” (Luke 13:3). Peter preached, “Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away” (Acts 3:19), and on the day of Pentecost, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38). True repentance is more than regret: “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). It shows in a changed life (Luke 3:8), it begins with confessing our sins, and God is faithful to forgive (1 John 1:9). Jesus said that there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:7).

entries.answer:
Scripture: John the Baptist said of Jesus, “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (Matthew 3:11). Before He ascended, Jesus told His disciples to wait for the gift the Father promised: “in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1:4-5), and “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses” (Acts 1:8). On the day of Pentecost “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them” (Acts 2:4). The Samaritans received the Spirit when Peter and John prayed and laid hands on them (Acts 8:14-17), the household of Cornelius when “they heard them speaking in tongues and exalting God” (Acts 10:44-46), and the disciples at Ephesus when “the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied” (Acts 19:1-6). Jesus said that the Father will give the Holy Spirit “to those who ask Him” (Luke 11:13), and Paul wrote, “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13).

Pentecostal understanding: the baptism in the Holy Spirit is a gift of Christ to believers, distinct from and following the new birth, to empower them for witness and service. The first sign of it, as at Pentecost, at Caesarea and at Ephesus, is speaking in other tongues as the Spirit gives utterance. It is promised to every believer (Acts 2:38-39), is received by asking in faith, and is followed by a life continually filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18).

Other views: most evangelical and Reformed teachers hold that every believer is baptized with the Spirit at conversion, citing 1 Corinthians 12:13, and that the Acts accounts describe unique moments as the gospel reached new peoples. They look for the Spirit's work in character and fruit rather than in tongues. The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches link the gift of the Spirit with baptism and confirmation or chrismation, and Catholic charismatics speak of a “release” of the Spirit received at baptism.

entries.answer: The Bible tells us not to worry, because God knows our needs and cares for us. Jesus said, “Do not worry about your life, what you will eat or drink; or about your body, what you will wear. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothes?” (Matthew 6:25), and, “But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you. Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Today has enough trouble of its own” (Matthew 6:33-34). Paul wrote, “Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:6-7). Peter says, “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). See also Psalm 55:22 and Isaiah 26:3. When worry grows into constant anxiety or depression, it is wise to seek a pastor and also medical help, as the Bible does not forbid this (Proverbs 11:14).

entries.answer:
Scripture: the Bible does not use the word abortion, but it speaks often of the child in the womb. David praises God: “You knit me together in my mother's womb... Your eyes saw my unformed body; all my days were written in Your book and ordained for me before one of them came to be” (Psalm 139:13-16). God told Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I set you apart” (Jeremiah 1:5), and when Mary greeted Elizabeth, “the baby leaped in her womb” (Luke 1:41). The command is “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13), and God hates “hands that shed innocent blood” (Proverbs 6:16-17). Exodus 21:22-25 speaks of men who strike a pregnant woman so that her child is born prematurely and requires payment for any harm that follows.

Pentecostal understanding: the unborn child is a person known and formed by God from conception, so abortion takes an innocent human life, and the Church should speak for the unborn (Proverbs 31:8) while showing compassion and practical help to mothers and families. Those who have had an abortion are not beyond forgiveness: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

Other views: the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches also teach that abortion is wrong from conception. Some Christians read Exodus 21:22-25 as treating the loss of an unborn child differently from the loss of a life and therefore hold that abortion may be allowed in limited cases, such as danger to the mother's life, and a few Christian bodies support legal access to abortion as a matter of conscience.

entries.answer: God told Moses His name at the burning bush: “I AM WHO I AM. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘I AM has sent me to you’”, and, “The LORD, the God of your fathers... has sent me to you. This is My name forever” (Exodus 3:14-15). Where English Bibles print LORD in capital letters, the Hebrew has God's personal name, four letters (YHWH), probably pronounced Yahweh. Out of reverence the Jews did not say it aloud and read Adonai (Lord) instead; “Jehovah” is an old English form made by joining the consonants of YHWH to the vowels of Adonai. God said, “I am the LORD; that is My name!” (Isaiah 42:8). Other names and titles in the Bible include Elohim (God, as in Genesis 1:1), El Shaddai (God Almighty, Genesis 17:1; Exodus 6:3), El Elyon (God Most High, Genesis 14:18-20) and Yahweh Yireh (“The LORD Will Provide”, Genesis 22:14). Jesus taught us to pray to “our Father” (Matthew 6:9), and the name of Jesus means that the LORD saves (Matthew 1:21).

entries.answer: The Bible does not say on what day, or in what month, Jesus was born. Luke tells us that there were “shepherds residing in the fields nearby, keeping watch over their flocks by night” (Luke 2:8), and that Mary gave birth in Bethlehem during a census (Luke 2:1-7), during the reign of King Herod (Matthew 2:1), but gives no date. Some think the shepherds point to a time other than midwinter, though others note that flocks could be kept out in the Judean winter. The earliest record of Christians keeping December 25 as the birth of Christ comes from Rome in the fourth century. Scholars are not agreed on why that date was chosen, some say it was calculated from the date of His conception or death, others that it replaced a pagan midwinter festival. The Bible gives no command to keep Christmas, and Paul writes that one person “regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” and that he who observes a special day “does so to the Lord” (Romans 14:5-6). Christians therefore differ on keeping it, but all can rejoice that the Savior was born.

entries.answer: Matthew tells us that “Magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem, asking, ‘Where is the One who has been born King of the Jews? We saw His star in the east and have come to worship Him’” (Matthew 2:1-2). Magi were learned men who studied the stars. Herod, told that the Christ would be born in Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), sent them there, and the star went ahead of them (Matthew 2:7-10). “On coming to the house, they saw the Child with His mother Mary, and they fell down and worshiped Him. Then they opened their treasures and presented Him with gifts of gold and frankincense and myrrh” (Matthew 2:11). Warned in a dream, they returned home another way (Matthew 2:12). The Bible does not say that there were three, it says only that there were three gifts; it does not call them kings or give their names. The names Caspar, Melchior and Balthazar come from later tradition. They found Jesus in a house, as a Child, not in the manger, and Herod, working from the time they gave him, had all the boys in Bethlehem “two years old and under” put to death (Matthew 2:16), so Jesus may have been up to two years old.

entries.answer: The Ark of the Covenant was the gold-covered wooden chest that God told Moses to make for the tabernacle (Exodus 25:10-22). Its lid, the mercy seat, was topped by two cherubim, and God said, “I will meet with you there above the mercy seat... I will speak with you about all that I command you” (Exodus 25:22). Inside were the stone tablets of the covenant, the gold jar of manna and Aaron's staff that had budded (Hebrews 9:4; 1 Kings 8:9). It went before Israel at the crossing of the Jordan (Joshua 3) and the fall of Jericho (Joshua 6), was captured by the Philistines (1 Samuel 4-6), and was brought to Jerusalem by David (2 Samuel 6) and placed in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:1-9). The last time the Bible mentions it on earth is when King Josiah told the Levites, “Put the holy ark in the temple built by Solomon” (2 Chronicles 35:3). When Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC the Bible does not say what became of it, and Jeremiah foretold that it would no longer be remembered (Jeremiah 3:16). Its fate is unknown. Some say it was destroyed or taken by the Babylonians, a Jewish writing outside the Bible says Jeremiah hid it (2 Maccabees 2:4-8), and the Ethiopian church claims to have it in Axum, but none of this can be proved. John saw “the ark of His covenant” in the temple of God in heaven (Revelation 11:19).

entries.answer: Passover is the feast that remembers how God freed Israel from slavery in Egypt. On the night of the tenth plague each family killed a lamb and put its blood on the doorposts, and God said, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you. No plague will fall on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt” (Exodus 12:1-13). God commanded, “this day will be a memorial for you, and you are to celebrate it as a feast to the LORD, as a permanent statute for the generations to come” (Exodus 12:14), on the fourteenth day of the first month (Leviticus 23:5), followed by the seven days of Unleavened Bread. Jesus kept the Passover with His disciples and said, “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering” (Luke 22:15), and at that meal gave the bread and the cup of the new covenant (Luke 22:19-20). He died at Passover time. John the Baptist called Him “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), and Paul writes, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Passover is therefore a picture of deliverance by the blood of the lamb.

entries.answer:
Scripture: slavery was a part of the ancient world, and the Bible speaks about it in several ways. God began Israel's story by freeing them from it: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). The law said, “Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death, whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession” (Exodus 21:16), set rules for servants including their release (Exodus 21:2-11; Leviticus 25:39-43), but also permitted buying servants from the surrounding nations (Leviticus 25:44). In the New Testament Paul lists “slave traders” among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10), tells masters to treat their slaves justly and to “Give up your use of threats” (Ephesians 6:9; Colossians 4:1), tells slaves who can gain freedom to take it (1 Corinthians 7:21), and asks Philemon to receive his runaway slave Onesimus “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:15-16). “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28).

Pentecostal understanding: the Bible did not invent slavery; it restrained it, condemned man-stealing and the trade in people, and taught that every person is made in God's image (Genesis 1:27) and is equal in Christ. Those truths led believers such as William Wilberforce to fight against the slave trade, and the Azusa Street revival of 1906, led by William Seymour, a son of former slaves, was notable for black and white believers worshipping together.

Other views: critics say that the Bible should have forbidden slavery outright, and that its laws allowing the purchase of foreigners (Leviticus 25:44-46) and the rules on beating slaves (Exodus 21:20-21) accept it. Scholars differ on how the servitude of Israelites, a kind of debt service, compares with the slavery of foreigners. Some people in the past used the Bible to defend slavery, and the Church has since repented of that.

entries.answer:
Scripture: the law of Moses listed clean and unclean animals, and pigs were unclean (Leviticus 11:2-8; Deuteronomy 14:3-8). After the flood God had told Noah that every moving thing that lives would be food for him (Genesis 9:3). Jesus said that nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him, because it goes into the stomach, and Mark adds, “Thus all foods are clean” (Mark 7:18-19). Peter was told in a vision, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean” (Acts 10:13-15). Paul wrote, “I am convinced and fully persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself” (Romans 14:14), and, “every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected, because it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (1 Timothy 4:4-5). The early church asked Gentile believers only to abstain from food polluted by idols, from the meat of strangled animals and from blood (Acts 15:19-20). We are not to judge one another over food (Romans 14:1-4; Colossians 2:16).

Pentecostal understanding: the food laws were part of the law that set Israel apart until Christ came; because Christ declared all foods clean, a Christian is free to eat pork and shellfish, giving thanks to God, and should not be judged over it.

Other views: Jewish people keep the kosher laws, as do some Messianic Jewish believers, Seventh-day Adventists, who teach that the distinction between clean and unclean animals still applies, and some other Christians who keep the Old Testament food laws. Some read Peter's vision as being mainly about accepting Gentile people (Acts 10:28) rather than about food.

entries.answer:
Scripture: from the beginning God joined one man to one woman: “a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), and Jesus quoted this when He taught on marriage (Matthew 19:4-6). The first man recorded with two wives was Lamech (Genesis 4:19). Abraham, Jacob, David and Solomon had more than one wife, and the Bible shows the trouble it caused, with jealousy in the households of Abraham and Jacob (Genesis 16; 29-30), and Solomon's wives turning his heart from God (1 Kings 11:1-4). The law told the king, “He must not take many wives for himself, lest his heart go astray” (Deuteronomy 17:17), and regulated the rights of wives in a household (Exodus 21:10). In the New Testament an overseer must be “the husband of but one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6).

Pentecostal understanding: God's design for marriage is one man and one woman for life. The Bible records the polygamy of the patriarchs and kings without approving of it, and its consequences warn against it. Marriage is a picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31-32).

Other views: some say that because the Old Testament law regulated rather than forbade plural marriage, and the New Testament rule on having one wife is given to church leaders, polygamy was tolerated for others. Churches in countries where polygamy is accepted differ on how to receive a man who already has several wives when he comes to faith: some ask him to stay with his family but not to take leadership, others ask that he not marry again.

entries.answer:
Scripture: as Jesus went up into heaven two angels said, “This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11). Jesus said that “the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven... They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven, with power and great glory” (Matthew 24:30). John writes, “Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him” (Revelation 1:7), and Paul calls it “the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13). “For the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will be the first to rise. After that, we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air” (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17). No one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), so we are to be ready (Matthew 24:42-44).

Pentecostal understanding: Christ will return in two stages: first He will come for His church, who will be caught up to meet Him in the air at the rapture; then, after the tribulation, He will come back to earth with His saints to defeat the Antichrist and reign for a thousand years (Zechariah 14:4; Revelation 19:11-16; 20:4-6).

Other views: some believe that the church will go through the tribulation and be caught up when Christ returns after it (a post-tribulation return), and many others (amillennialists) teach that He returns once, at the end of history, to raise the dead, judge all people and make all things new. All Christians agree that Jesus will return in glory and that the dead will be raised.

entries.answer:
Scripture: when the Lamb opened the first four of the seven seals, four horses came out (Revelation 6:1-8). The first was a white horse whose rider “held a bow. And he was given a crown, and he rode out to overcome and conquer.” The second was bright red, and its rider “was granted permission to take away peace from the earth and to make men slay one another.” The third was black, and its rider held a pair of scales, with the price of food rising: “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius.” The fourth was a pale green horse, whose rider's name “was Death, and Hades followed close behind. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill by sword, by famine, by plague, and by the beasts of the earth.”

Pentecostal understanding: the seals are judgments of the future tribulation, which follows the rapture of the church. The white horseman is the Antichrist, who comes as a conqueror and a counterfeit of Christ, and who is not to be confused with the rider on the white horse in Revelation 19:11, “Faithful and True.” The other three bring war, famine and death.

Other views: some Christians think the white horse is Christ, or the spread of the gospel, with the other three horsemen as the sufferings that accompany it. Others see all four as symbols of conquest, war, famine and death that have recurred throughout history, or as events of the first century, and some take them as a picture of the whole age between Christ's two comings.

entries.answer:
Scripture: John heard an angel say, “Do not harm the land or sea or trees until we have sealed the foreheads of the servants of our God,” and heard the number of those sealed, “144,000 from all the tribes of Israel” (Revelation 7:3-4), with twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes (Revelation 7:5-8). Later he saw “the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with Him 144,000 who had His name and His Father's name written on their foreheads” (Revelation 14:1). They sing a new song before the throne, they “follow the Lamb wherever He goes,” and they “have been redeemed from among men as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb” (Revelation 14:3-4). “No lie was found in their mouths; they are blameless” (Revelation 14:5).

Pentecostal understanding: the 144,000 are Jewish believers, twelve thousand from each tribe of Israel, who are sealed by God for protection and witness during the tribulation, and who are followed by a multitude from every nation (Revelation 7:9). They are a picture of God keeping His promises to Israel (Romans 11:25-29).

Other views: many Christians read the number as a symbol, twelve times twelve times a thousand, for the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile, complete and protected (compare Galatians 6:16). The Jehovah's Witnesses teach that 144,000 is the literal number of believers who go to heaven, while the rest of the faithful live on a restored earth; most other Christians do not accept this, since the Bible also speaks of a countless multitude before the throne (Revelation 7:9).

entries.question: What does Selah mean?
alt_phrasings: what is selah in the psalms

entries.answer: Selah is a Hebrew word found 71 times in the Psalms and three times in Habakkuk 3 (verses 3, 9, 13). An example is “Many say of me, ‘God will not deliver him.’ Selah” (Psalm 3:2). The Bible does not explain it. It probably was a direction to the singers or musicians, and most commonly it is taken to mean a pause: to stop and think about what has just been said, or to lift up the voice, or a musical interlude. The old Greek translation of the Psalms treats it as a musical break. Because nobody is certain, translators leave the word as it is.

entries.answer: Hallelujah is a Hebrew word meaning “Praise the LORD”: hallelu is the command to praise, and Yah is the short form of the LORD's name (Yahweh). It begins and ends many psalms, for example, “Hallelujah! Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever” (Psalm 106:1; see also Psalms 111-113; 146-150). In the New Testament the word appears only in Revelation 19, where a great multitude in heaven shouts, “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God!” (Revelation 19:1; see also verses 3, 4 and 6). Some Bibles translate it as “Praise the LORD” or “Praise Yah”.

entries.answer: Immanuel is a Hebrew name meaning “God with us.” Isaiah told King Ahaz, “the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel” (Isaiah 7:14). Matthew applies it to the birth of Jesus: “they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”) (Matthew 1:22-23). It tells us that in Jesus, God Himself came to live among His people (John 1:14), and Jesus ended His Gospel with the promise, “I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Emmanuel is the Greek spelling of the same name.

entries.answer: Abba is the Aramaic word for father. Jesus prayed in Gethsemane, “Abba, Father,” He said, “all things are possible for You. Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will” (Mark 14:36). Paul says that believers “did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of sonship, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15), and “because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, ‘Abba, Father!’” (Galatians 4:6). The word expresses the trust and closeness of a child to a father. It is often said to mean “daddy”, but scholars point out that it was also used by grown sons and daughters, so it is better understood as “my Father”, said with love and respect. It is the Holy Spirit who enables us to speak to God in this way.

entries.answer: Mary Magdalene, that is, Mary of Magdala, a town on the Sea of Galilee, was a follower of Jesus: “Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out,” who with other women supported Jesus and the Twelve out of their own means (Luke 8:2-3). She watched the crucifixion, with other women (Mark 15:40; John 19:25) and saw where He was buried (Mark 15:47). Early on the first day of the week she went to the tomb and found the stone removed (John 20:1). The risen Jesus appeared first to her, called her by name, and sent her to tell the disciples; she announced, “I have seen the Lord!” (John 20:11-18; Mark 16:9). The Bible never says she was a prostitute. The idea that she was the sinful woman of Luke 7:36-50 comes from a sermon by Pope Gregory in AD 591, and the Catholic Church dropped it in 1969. The Bible also does not say she married Jesus, and no early source says so.

entries.answer:
Scripture: when Abram returned from defeating the kings, “Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine, since he was priest of God Most High, and he blessed Abram” and Abram gave him a tenth of everything (Genesis 14:18-20). David foretold of the Messiah, “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4). The letter to the Hebrews explains that his name means king of righteousness and king of peace, and that “without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time” (Hebrews 7:1-3). Jesus is a priest in his order (Hebrews 5:10; 6:20), greater than the Levitical priests because Levi himself, in Abraham, paid tithes to Melchizedek (Hebrews 7:4-10).

Pentecostal understanding: Melchizedek was a real king and priest of Salem, later Jerusalem, who served the one true God, and he is a picture of Christ, the King of righteousness and peace and a priest who lasts forever, appointed not by descent but by God's oath (Hebrews 7:11-22).

Other views: some teachers hold that he was an appearance of the Son of God before He was born as a man (a Christophany). Jewish tradition identified him with Shem, the son of Noah. Others think Hebrews says that he is “like” the Son of God, so he is a type of Christ rather than Christ Himself, and that the details about no beginning or end refer to the silence of Scripture about his birth and death.

entries.answer: Abraham, first called Abram, was born in Ur of the Chaldeans, the son of Terah (Genesis 11:26-31). God called him to leave his country and promised, “I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing... and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:2-3). He went to Canaan, and God made a covenant with him. “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). God changed his name: “No longer will you be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations” (Genesis 17:5). His sons were Ishmael, by Sarah's servant Hagar, and Isaac, the son of promise, born to Sarah when Abraham was a hundred (Genesis 16; 21). God tested him by asking him to offer Isaac, and provided a ram instead (Genesis 22). He died at 175 years old (Genesis 25:7-8). The New Testament calls him the father of all who believe (Romans 4:11-12; Galatians 3:7-9); James adds that “he was called a friend of God” (James 2:23).

entries.answer: Paul, also called Saul, was a Jew “born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but raised in” Jerusalem and “educated at the feet of Gamaliel in strict conformity to the law” (Acts 22:3). He was of the tribe of Benjamin, “a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; as to zeal, persecuting the church” (Philippians 3:5-6). He approved of Stephen's death and set out to arrest believers in Damascus, but the risen Jesus appeared to him on the road (Acts 7:58; 9:1-9). The Lord said of him, “This man is My chosen instrument to carry My name before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel” (Acts 9:15). He was baptized, and made three missionary journeys, planting churches in Asia Minor, Macedonia and Greece (Acts 13-21). He was arrested in Jerusalem and sent to Rome (Acts 21-28). He wrote thirteen letters of the New Testament (Romans through Philemon), and tradition says he was put to death in Rome under Nero. He wrote near the end of his life, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7).

entries.answer:
Scripture: Simon, son of John (or Jonah), was a fisherman from Bethsaida, brought to Jesus by his brother Andrew, and Jesus named him Cephas, in Greek Peter, which means rock (John 1:40-42). When Jesus asked who the disciples said He was, “Simon Peter answered, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’” Jesus replied, “And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:16-19). He walked on the water (Matthew 14:28-31), was at the transfiguration, denied Jesus three times (Luke 22:54-62), and was restored by the risen Lord, who said three times, “Feed My sheep” (John 21:15-17). On the day of Pentecost he preached and about three thousand were baptized (Acts 2:14-41); he first took the gospel to the Gentiles at the house of Cornelius (Acts 10). He wrote 1 and 2 Peter. Tradition says he was crucified in Rome.

Pentecostal understanding: the rock on which Christ builds His church is the truth Peter confessed, that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Christ Himself is the foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11; 1 Peter 2:4-8; Ephesians 2:20). Peter was a leading apostle and a pastor of the church, and an elder among elders (1 Peter 5:1), but not a ruler over the others.

Other views: the Roman Catholic Church teaches that Jesus made Peter the first pope and that his authority passes to the bishops of Rome. The Eastern Orthodox Church honours Peter as first among the apostles but does not give the bishop of Rome authority over the other churches.

entries.answer: Jacob was the younger twin son of Isaac and Rebekah; he was born holding his brother Esau's heel, hence his name, which sounds like heel (Genesis 25:24-26). He bought Esau's birthright for a bowl of stew (Genesis 25:29-34), and with Rebekah's help took Isaac's blessing by deceit (Genesis 27), and fled from Esau to his uncle Laban. At Bethel he dreamed of a ladder to heaven, and God promised, “I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land” (Genesis 28:10-15). He worked fourteen years for Rachel and Leah (Genesis 29), and had twelve sons by them and their servants, who became the twelve tribes of Israel (Genesis 29-30; 35:22-26). Returning home, he wrestled with a man at Peniel, who said, “Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed” (Genesis 32:24-30). He loved Joseph most, grieved when he was lost, and moved to Egypt when Joseph became ruler there, where he died at 147 and was buried in Canaan (Genesis 37; 46-50).
